<reason>Both sides built coherent cases — CON on employer discretion, litigation costs falling on small business, and the vagueness of "materially"; PRO on the contract-for-labor framing, the chilling effect of unreviewable firing power, and the observation that the motion's own materiality clause already limits its scope. The pivotal exchange was PRO's pressure question demanding a concrete case of lawful, job-irrelevant conduct that still justifies firing. CON's answer (the gambling bookkeeper, the "reputational risk" hire) actually smuggled in forward-looking risk rather than genuine irrelevance, which let PRO's closing show that CON's own "prudent risk management" standard cannot reliably distinguish legitimate business judgment from bare prejudice — a point CON's final speech answered only by asserting "redefinition" rather than rebutting the mechanism. PRO also more effectively exploited the tension in CON's position (praising narrow protected-class statutes while insisting on unlimited employer discretion), and its analogy to existing judgment-laden legal standards (BFOQ, undue hardship) blunted CON's "materially is undefinable" attack. CON's rebuttals were solid and the asymmetry/administrability arguments landed some real damage, but PRO's line of attack stayed sharper and more decisive across rounds, and PRO adapted the debate toward the cleaner dispositive question more successfully.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question ("name one case that is lawful, off-duty, and genuinely irrelevant, yet firing is still deserved") combined with its closing turn of CON's bookkeeper/reputational-risk answer into "cannot distinguish prudence from prejudice" was the most decisive exchange; CON's response that this was "redefinition, not rebuttal" did not fully neutralize it.</best_rebuttal>
